Common names can be confusing and vary by language, so scientific names help scientists clearly identify organisms. Binomial nomenclature is a system that gives each species a two-part name: the genus and the specific name. Scientists use shared and unique traits to classify organisms and give each species its own scientific name.

Taxonomy helps scientists group and name organisms based on shared and unique traits, even when common names are confusing. By comparing traits, scientists organize organisms into different levels of classification, from broad domains and kingdoms to specific species. These groups help scientists compare organisms and understand the different roles they play in ecosystems.

Trait variation influences fitness by affecting how well organisms survive and reproduce in different environments. Whether inherited traits are advantageous or disadvantageous depends on the environment—and when the environment changes. As a result, how common or rare inherited traits are in a population can change over time.

Traits explain both the similarities and differences among individuals of the same species. Inherited traits, acquired traits, and learned behaviors describe different ways an organism's characteristics are inherited or may develop over an organism’s lifetime. Fitness and trait variation help explain how inherited traits influence survival, reproduction, and changes in populations over time.
